title: Chapter 153: Jiujiang Third Psychological Convalescence Centre
html:
No one in Liu Dao’s studio had ever been asked such a question, and the crew fell speechless. At last, Liu Dao stepped forward. “Be careful tonight. Safety comes first. We surveyed the hospital grounds while it was still light.”

“You went inside? What did you find?” The intensity of Chen Ge’s stare made Liu Dao uncomfortable.

“We only walked around the perimeter. We didn’t dare enter. But I downloaded a map of the hospital that was supposedly drawn by one of its patients.” Liu Dao opened a file on his laptop, revealing a crude floor plan. “The complex contains three interconnected buildings.

“The first and second sick halls housed ordinary patients, with entrances and windows facing the sun. The Third Sick Hall was more secretive. It served as an isolation ward for the most dangerous patients, and its doors and windows faced away from the sun.

“You must be extremely careful near it. According to the patient who drew this map, ordinary patients were forbidden from approaching the Third Sick Hall. Anyone caught nearby received a terrible punishment.

“I suggest you avoid it tonight. If you take your time, the first two halls should provide more than enough material.”

Liu Dao turned the screen toward Chen Ge so he could memorize the map.

“Is the Third Sick Hall truly that unusual? Did you find anything else about it online?” Chen Ge asked, his expression grave.

“Not much, and some stories sounded fabricated. One claimed that the patients murdered a doctor and that no one discovered the crime for several days. Another insisted the building housed strange creatures rather than human beings.” Liu Dao laughed uneasily. “That has to be fiction, right?”

He closed the laptop. Everyone noticed the shift in Chen Ge’s demeanor; something had left him deeply troubled.

“Check the cameras. We don’t have much time.” Chen Ge shouldered his backpack, fastened the chest and wrist cameras, and attached the audio recorder. After testing them all, he headed out of the tent.

“If it gets too dangerous, turn around and run. Mark your route, and set my number as your emergency contact,” Liu Dao called after him. “I’ll phone one minute before the broadcast begins. You can monitor the feed from your own livestream room. And remember, no one has entered that place in years. I can’t promise what you’ll find. Be careful!”

The man’s concern surprised Chen Ge. At the tent entrance, he set Liu Dao as his emergency contact where everyone could see, then waved. “Stay inside the tent. Don’t wander, and no matter what you see or hear, don’t come looking for me. Understood?”

“But if…”

“Take care of the equipment. Leave the content to me.” Man and cat vanished into the darkness.

Sister Lee watched him leave with her arms folded, her earlier doubts still unresolved. Under her breath, she admitted, “At least he looks rather handsome from behind.”

Chen Ge was more nervous than anyone realized. This was his first genuine Three-Star scenario, and he understood its danger. He also knew that the stories Liu Dao dismissed as inventions were likely true. Perhaps the patient who drew the map had been confined precisely because he could see what ordinary people could not.

Following the map from memory, he reached the far edge of the woods, where an old compound emerged from the darkness.

“The hospital is enormous.” Hearing that it was privately operated, he had imagined a cramped, miserable institution capable of housing only a handful of patients. Seeing it in person proved how wrong he had been.

Dense woods encircled the grounds, and the only entrance had been sealed. High concrete walls hid everything beyond them. As Chen Ge approached, however, he noticed something unsettling.

Senseless sentences covered the concrete, all sharing one feature: each mentioned someone’s name. He initially tried to memorize them, but there were too many sentences, too many names, and too many repetitions. Eventually, he gave up.

Do these names belong to the hospital’s patients?

The sentences made no sense to him, yet their strangeness was undeniable.

No ordinary person wrote these. What were they trying to communicate?

As he studied the wall, unease crept over him. The words felt like curses aimed directly at their reader. “White Tiger, stay close.”

With no one else around, using the grandiose name no longer embarrassed him. The nearer they drew to the hospital, the more hostile the white cat became. Sensitive to unnatural presences, it had clearly detected something.

“Don’t worry. We have our own advantages.” Chen Ge raised the rooster dangling from its bound legs and drew his mallet. Rather than enter immediately, he waited for Liu Dao’s call.

“The equipment is working well; the picture is clear and stable. We’ve started the livestream. You can check it out on your own phone.”

“All right.” Chen Ge logged onto the platform and immediately saw an advertisement for Qin Guang’s stream. He opened it. Qin Guang’s team had suffered a minor accident outside Mu Yang High School: their equipment van had apparently run into a ditch. In a live apology, Qin Guang explained that something had fallen across the windshield and distracted the driver.

They truly went to Mu Yang High School. He ignored my warning. Still, even this apology has almost four hundred thousand viewers. I can’t underestimate him.

Chen Ge switched to his own livestream room. Thanks to the platform recommendation, its audience quickly climbed to 250,000.

The broadcast displayed several feeds. The largest and clearest came from the chest camera. A smaller window in the lower-left corner showed his wrist camera, whose angle he could adjust like a watch. Raising his arm even allowed him to view his own body on-screen.

Ten o’clock. Time to begin.

He aimed the wrist camera at his face and glanced at the rapidly scrolling chat. “I never expected to do anything this crazy tonight.”

After patting his backpack and helping the white cat onto the wall, Chen Ge climbed into the Jiujiang Third Psychological Convalescence Centre.
